body_en:
He Zhili, at the 1987 World Championships. Her coach told her to throw the match. She didn't. She played, she won, she took the title. Then she was struck from the team.

Jiao Zhimin threw five matches in eight years on the international stage. After the fifth, she stood on the bronze-medal podium and cried. Back home, a team leader told her, "You're leading the way." She said, "Don't you find that hypocritical?" Then she retired.

Fan Zhendong — the WTT said skip a tournament and get fined, so he signed the withdrawal papers. But he didn't retire. He went to the German league, played at a 92% win rate, and won a treble.

Boza, a journalist, 71 years old, asked at a World Championships press conference in London the question everyone wanted to ask but no one dared to. A staffer said, "That's not a question." He said, "I'll keep asking."

Four people, four eras, four choices.

He Zhili chose to win. The price was being erased by her own country and called a traitor for thirty years. She later moved to Japan, changed her name to Koyama Chire, and at the 1994 Asian Games, playing for Japan, beat Deng Yaping. Public opinion back home nailed her to a pillar of shame. But one thing rarely gets mentioned: the decision that made her throw that match was later expressly banned by the sports commission. The system changed. Her reputation never recovered. And the people who changed the system never thanked her.

Jiao Zhimin chose to leave. She married and moved to South Korea, and never represented any country in competition again. Years later, in an interview, she said, "Athletes today are so lucky — they don't have to throw matches; they can fight for the title on their own merit." She said it calmly. But she probably didn't know that in 2024, another Chinese athlete was forced to sign a withdrawal document for refusing to be bound by the rules. She thought that once match-throwing was gone, everything would be fine.

Fan Zhendong chose silence. He didn't denounce the WTT, didn't publicly criticize anyone, didn't write long posts on social media. He just went to Germany, played, won, and took titles. He won quietly. He lost quietly too. Some called him a traitor; he didn't respond. Some cried injustice on his behalf; he didn't share their posts. The only emotional words he ever spoke were: "There's no room left at all. I tried to talk myself through it, but every road is blocked." And after saying that, he kept playing.

Boza chose to speak. When everyone else kept quiet, a 71-year-old Italian man who had never met Fan Zhendong stood up at a press conference where he could have simply filed his story and gone home, and asked that question in front of the whole world. He said later: "I have never spoken with Fan Zhendong. I don't even know whether he knows who I am. He isn't even my favorite player." He didn't ask because he liked him. He asked because that was his job.
excerpt_en: He Zhili refused to throw a match and was erased. Jiao Zhimin threw five and walked away. Fan Zhendong signed his way out and won in silence. And a 71-year-old Italian journalist asked the question no one else dared to.
title_en: Four People, Four Acts of Defiance
